web_evidence.title: Toni Morrison's Fiction: Contemporary Criticism
web_evidence.note: The academic collection's Bluest Eye discussion states that some sections are first person with Claudia as a character while others are third-person omniscient; it ultimately interprets both as manifestations of the same teller, which does not erase the sustained grammatical-person alternation.

web_evidence.title: Fragmented Identities in Selected Novels by V. S. Naipaul and Toni Morrison
web_evidence.note: University-hosted scholarship explicitly describes four seasonal sections narrated in first person by Claudia, primer sections using other voices, and a double first-/third-person point of view.

web_evidence.title: Blues, Jazz, and Embodiment in Toni Morrison's The Bluest Eye
web_evidence.note: The graduate journal traces section-level switches from Claudia's first person to semi-omniscient third person across Autumn, Winter, Spring, and Summer, while distinguishing Pauline's interspersed first-person reflections and Pecola's final dialogue.

web_evidence.title: The Bluest Eye
web_evidence.note: The reference essay identifies adult and child Claudia's first-person narration, an anonymous omniscient third-person narrator, third-person biographies of Cholly and Pauline, and Pauline's embedded first-person passages.

person_note: The novel contains sustained narration in more than one grammatical person: Claudia participates as an “I/we” narrator in the seasonal and framing material, while substantial primer-headed sections use omniscient third-person narration for the Breedloves, Cholly, Geraldine, and Soaphead. The quote set independently exhibits both strands, and multiple scholarly structural sources confirm their section-level alternation. Pauline's first-person reminiscences, Soaphead's letter, and Pecola's imagined dialogue are local embedded voices and do not independently determine the book label. Some criticism treats the third-person voice as adult Claudia's expanded authorial voice, but under this methodology a shared implied teller does not negate sustained first-/third-person section shifts. The main residual uncertainty concerns that theoretical identity of the voices, not the observable alternating-person structure.
